description:
We are a team of two developers passionate about technology, programming, and space exploration. We enjoy solving challenging problems, building interactive applications, and turning creative ideas into working projects.

Our goal is to combine our technical skills and creativity to develop an innovative and useful solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary: A satellite map is silent for people who are blind or have low vision. Earth Jukebox lets anyone hear NASA Earth data in the browser: pick one of eleven visualizations, move across it with the keyboard, a mouse or the arrow buttons, and every region speaks through pitch, loudness, rhythm and timbre, with the same reading shown as text. One map is built straight from measured NASA sea surface temperatures, so its pitch is in real degrees Celsius. Any map can also become a 15 second song, and a jukebox plays them all. The whole player works in English and Ukrainian.
details:
What it does. Choose a visualization and press Play, or move region by region. Night lights for the world, Ukraine and India sound louder where they are brighter, and in Change mode a high note means brighter since 2012 and a low note darker. Measured sea temperature from NASA JPL's MUR analysis on 15 July 2023 rises about one semitone per degree Celsius, from 110 Hz at −2 °C to 880 Hz at 32 °C. Ocean currents, Saharan dust, carbon dioxide, forest height, an atmospheric river and air quality each have their own mapping, explained on the page. NOAA GOES-16 lightning plays one click at the real time of every flash recorded in the same minute near Cuba (88 flashes) and over the Central Great Plains (20).

Accessibility. Every control is a native button or slider with a label. Each region's reading is announced as text, a text summary lists the strongest and weakest regions of any map, two listening stops per map can be played back to back, and keyboard shortcuts cover playing, moving, restarting and comparing. Sound can be downloaded as WAV for offline listening.

Music and play. Any map becomes a 15 second stereo song: the readings are the melody, bass and texture, rounded to a scale. A jukebox plays a song from every map in a row, and dragging across a map with a mouse plays it like an instrument. The music page compares a finished song with the same data in the player's unchanged sounds.

How it works. A static site with no server or API keys. HTML Canvas reads 8 by 4 regions of each NASA frame; Web Audio synthesizes tones, noise and clicks. The sea temperature track uses a 2 degree subset of the MUR SST v4.1 analysis, averaged by region and weighted by latitude. Eighteen automated tests check the mappings, the data subsets, the music generator and the Ukrainian text.

Honest limits. Except for sea temperature and lightning, readings come from the colors of rendered NASA visualizations, so they are relative and the page says so. We checked keyboard-only use, the accessibility tree and the spoken status messages in both languages, but we have not yet tested the player with a blind or low-vision user.

Local impact. Our team is from Ukraine. The Ukraine at night map lets listeners hear where the country got darker between 2012 and 2023, and the Ukrainian interface makes the tool usable in Ukrainian schools and by blind and low-vision communities.
